messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: separating concerns in RStan (and Stan)
parts:
(This is in response to a feature request I put in for
RStan to separate out a model object.)

The reason to separate model and fit is that they're
different concepts. The benefit of modularity is
in testing, documentation, and independent use.

I would like to see a model object in R that's a thin
wrapper around the model class in C++. This is just
used to provide the functions provided by the C++ class.
This is Stan-specific.

A bunch of Markov chains with variable names is a different
concept, and it's independent of how it's generated. This
concept is not Stan specific. So I still think it'd be nice
to allow other programs to use the R-hat and n_eff calcs
and nice summary output and graphics.

The fit object for ordinary MCMC sampling would then be a combination of
these two things. A fit object for optimization could be
something else. A fit object for variational Bayes could be
yet a different thing.

I do realize this can cause some redundancy in storing
variable names, but I think it's worth it for the separation.
(I don't know if R lets you store references or it it'll just
make a copy; either way, even a copy of all the names and
dimensions wouldn't be much overhead.)

This is not for RStan 2.0 by the way. I think it might make most
sense to do this when we add variational inference or a different
kind of sampler, etc. That'll give us an even better idea of
the functionality we need.

- Bob

On Sunday, September 29, 2013 6:49:30 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
(This is in response to a feature request I put in for

The reason to separate model and fit is that they're
different concepts.  The benefit of modularity is
in testing, documentation, and independent use.

I would like to see a model object in R that's a thin
wrapper around the model class in C++.  This is just
used to provide the functions provided by the C++ class.
This is Stan-specific.

There is exactly that already. It is called the stanmodel class and its documentation can be found from

help("stanmodel-class")

And an instance of class stanmodel is a slot of the stanfit class

> showClass("stanfit")
Class "stanfit" [package "rstan"]

Slots:
                                                                                                     
Name:   model_name  model_pars    par_dims        mode         sim       inits   stan_args   stanmodel
Class:   character   character        list     integer        list        list        list   stanmodel
                             
Name:         date       .MISC
Class:   character environment

The fit object for ordinary MCMC sampling would then be a combination of
these two things.   A fit object for optimization could be
something else.  A fit object for variational Bayes could be
yet a different thing.
These could all be subclasses of the stanfit class.

I do realize this can cause some redundancy in storing
variable names, but I think it's worth it for the separation.
(I don't know if R lets you store references or it it'll just
make a copy;  either way, even a copy of all the names and
dimensions wouldn't be much overhead.)

Most of the time, copies only happen on modification, which would be pretty rare in typical RStan useage.

Ben

Hi,

Even after spending plenty of time in the rstan code I find it challenging
keeping things straight. Please correct me if I've got the details wrong here.

There's a stan_fit C++ class, an R stan_fit class (I found myself wishing these
didn't have the same name). Then there's an R stan_model class and there's also
a stan_model<.......> C++ class.

There's other small sources of confusion such as, log_prob of the *model* is
exposed in the stan_fit C++ object.

In PyStan there's only a single stan_fit class. It *is* the C++ and Python class
simultaneously since Cython lets you tack on Python objects to C++ instances.
This turns out to be have been a mistake for parallel processing, so I'm going
to have to rewrite things along RStan lines. But at least the separation between
the classes will be clear since Python uses CamelCase. The Python classes are
StanModel and StanFit; the C++ classes are stan_model<....> and stan_fit.

Best,

Allen

On 9/30/13 9:03 AM, Allen Riddell wrote:
> Hi,

I hope Jiqiang can help with code details. Everything below
from me is just a design comment (with a hedge about C++ and
Python coding conventions, neither of which I know).

> There's a stan_fit C++ class, an R stan_fit class (I found myself wishing these
> didn't have the same name). Then there's an R stan_model class and there's also
> a stan_model<.......> C++ class.

I like the name parallelism as long as the R class is just
a thin wrapper around the C++ class, perhaps with some
utility methods attached related to R.

> There's other small sources of confusion such as, log_prob of the *model* is
> exposed in the stan_fit C++ object.

This is something that makes most sense to me to have
on the model class. The fit holds a reference to the model
class, so the way I'd like to see it used is to get the model
from the fit, then evaluate the log prob with the model.

But R has what seem to me a number of unusual conventions.
It's more conventional to have a very large function with
all kinds of configuation defaults and dependencies than a bunch
of modular building blocks. And in many ways this makes sense
for the call to the sampler, which has all kinds of config attached
to it, all of which has a default behavior.

> In PyStan there's only a single stan_fit class. It *is* the C++ and Python class
> simultaneously since Cython lets you tack on Python objects to C++ instances.
> This turns out to be have been a mistake for parallel processing, so I'm going
> to have to rewrite things along RStan lines. But at least the separation between
> the classes will be clear since Python uses CamelCase. The Python classes are
> StanModel and StanFit; the C++ classes are stan_model<....> and stan_fit.

I did Java for 10 years, so I kind of miss camel case.
Most C++ doesn't even use capital letters.

- Bob

Another thing that is confusing at the moment, is that if someone wants to use a parameterized precision matrix, they have to declare it as a cov_matrix:

}

  ...
}
